title: What Is Business English and Who Are Your Learners?
brief: Define Business English as a specialization focused on the language professionals need to function effectively in workplace contexts, distinguishing it from general English by its emphasis on specific communicative goals rather than broad language development. Describe the typical Business English learner: an adult with existing professional responsibilities, limited study time, clear instrumental motivation, and often a higher level of general English than a beginner class student. Explain that these learners bring valuable world knowledge and professional experience to lessons, which the teacher should treat as a resource rather than an obstacle. Introduce the idea that Business English lessons commonly address skills such as writing professional emails, participating in meetings, delivering presentations, and handling telephone calls or negotiations.

title: Conducting a Needs Analysis
brief: Explain that a needs analysis is the essential first step before planning any Business English course, because professional learners have highly specific goals that vary enormously from one client to the next. Describe the two main dimensions a needs analysis should explore: present situation (what the learner can already do in English at work) and target situation (what they need to be able to do, and in which contexts). Give practical guidance on how a teacher might gather this information — through a pre-course questionnaire, an initial interview, or a sample task such as asking the learner to write a short work email or describe a recent meeting in English. Stress that the needs analysis should also uncover constraints such as how many hours per week the learner can commit, whether lessons will be in-company or online, and any upcoming deadlines such as a conference or job interview that should shape lesson priorities.

title: Planning and Delivering Business English Lessons
brief: Explain how the findings of the needs analysis translate directly into lesson content, so that a learner who needs to chair meetings will practise turn-taking language and interrupting politely, while a learner who writes reports will work on formal register, cohesion, and hedging language. Provide two or three invented classroom examples — for instance, a role-play in which the learner practises opening a video call with a new client, or a writing task in which they redraft an overly informal email into an appropriate professional register. Discuss the importance of using authentic or realistic materials drawn from the learner's own workplace where possible, such as anonymised emails the learner has actually received, because this keeps content immediately relevant and motivating. Note that grammar and vocabulary are still taught explicitly when needed, but always in service of a communicative workplace goal rather than as ends in themselves.

title: Introduction to One-to-One Teaching
brief: Define one-to-one teaching as any lesson in which a single teacher works with a single student, and note that this format is extremely common in Business English but also occurs in general English, exam preparation, and young learner contexts. Explain the core ways in which one-to-one teaching differs from group teaching: there is no peer interaction to fall back on, the teacher cannot divide attention across multiple students, every silence or difficulty is immediately visible, and the entire communicative load of the lesson falls on two people. Describe the particular intensity this creates for both parties — the learner cannot hide behind classmates and receives constant personalised attention, while the teacher must sustain engagement and vary activity types more actively than in a group setting. Introduce the idea that one-to-one lessons demand a higher degree of flexibility and responsiveness than group lessons, because there is no class dynamic to carry momentum.

title: Pacing, Rapport, and Tailoring the One-to-One Lesson
brief: Discuss pacing as one of the most important practical skills in one-to-one teaching: the teacher must read the learner's energy and concentration levels continuously and be prepared to slow down, take a short break, switch activity type, or abandon a planned task if the learner is fatigued or disengaged. Explain that rapport in one-to-one teaching is both an asset and a responsibility — a strong working relationship makes the learner more willing to take risks and make mistakes, but the teacher must maintain a professional boundary so that lessons do not drift into unfocused conversation. Give concrete advice on tailoring: keeping a running record of recurring errors, noting topics and task types the learner responds well to, and revisiting language from previous lessons in new contexts so that learning is consolidated over time. Use an invented example such as a teacher noticing that a learner consistently confuses the present perfect and simple past in spoken production, and building a short recycling activity into the following three lessons to address this systematically.

title: Practical Challenges and Professional Habits for the Specialist Teacher
brief: Address the practical challenges that new teachers commonly face when moving into Business English or one-to-one work, including feeling underprepared for professional subject matter, managing lessons that run in the learner's workplace with frequent interruptions, and handling a learner who is significantly more senior or experienced professionally than the teacher. Reassure the reader that the teacher's role is language expert, not business consultant, and that it is entirely appropriate to ask the learner to explain their industry or role so that the teacher can contextualise language work accurately. Recommend professional habits that support quality in both specializations: writing brief lesson notes after each session to track what was covered and what needs revisiting, setting clear short-term goals with the learner at the start of a course and reviewing progress regularly, and being transparent with the learner about the lesson plan so they feel ownership of their own learning. Close by framing both Business English and one-to-one teaching as rewarding contexts in which a teacher can develop highly refined observation and responsiveness skills that benefit all their other teaching.
